The khim, the Thai hammered dulcimer, is a chordophone common in Indochina, similar to the hammered dulcimer or the cimbalom and introduced by way of the Chinese yangqin, which descends from the Mesopotamian or Persian santur. The body is of wood, with brass strings laid across it and two bridges; according to the model it has seven, nine, eleven or fifteen notes with three strings to a note, commonly forty-two strings. The player strikes the strings with two bamboo mallets with soft leather heads, sitting on the floor or on a chair, or standing before a stand. It has been used with Chinese opera troupes, and appears in Thai music curricula, with children beginning to learn, and in professional settings.
初學可選兩橋、七音、四十二弦的琴，為初級學生常用。演奏時將琴置於地面，或放於琴架: A beginner may choose a two-bridge, seven-note, forty-two-string instrument, which is what elementary students usually play. To play, set the instrument on the floor or on a stand and sit or stand; strike the courses of strings with two bamboo beaters with soft leather heads. To tune, turn the tuning pins on the right with a wrench and never those on the left, or the string will break; tighten or loosen to the pitch you need.
